name: Sharper Image
tierWhy: The stores were liquidated in 2008 and the company renamed itself TSIC, Inc., but the name was sold. It changed hands twice more, for $65.7M in 2011 and $100M in 2016, and sharperimage.com was still selling gadgets in October 2026.[^11][^13][^14][^15]

title: Sharper Image (1977–2008): post-mortem · Spectre Brands
description: The gadget catalog that became a mall chain of 190 stores, then came to depend on one air purifier. A sourced post-mortem of Sharper Image, built from its SEC filings, court coverage and the later sales of its name.

card.blurb: A San Francisco gadget catalog that became a mall fixture. By 2004 its Ionic Breeze air purifiers were 40% of revenue; when Consumer Reports panned them and sales fell away, the chain went bankrupt in 2008.

stat.label: of fiscal 2004 revenue came from one product line: air purifiers

hero.standfirst: It sold the things nobody needed but everybody wanted to try in the mall. Then it sold mostly one thing.
hero.deck: Sharper Image began in 1977 with a runner’s watch advertised in a magazine, mailed its first catalog in 1979 and opened stores in 1981. By fiscal 2004 it had 175 stores and $760M of revenue, and 40% of that came from its own fanless Ionic Breeze air purifiers. Consumer Reports said the purifiers did little; the company sued and lost. Air-purifier sales collapsed, revenue fell by almost a third in two years, a shareholder forced the founder out in 2006, and in February 2008 the company filed for Chapter 11. The stores were liquidated; the name lived on as a licence. This page is built from its SEC filings, court coverage in the Los Angeles Times, and the filings of the companies that bought the brand.

findings.title: One product carried the company.
findings.text: Air purifiers were 40.0% of revenue in fiscal 2004, 27.7% in 2005 and 23.4% in 2006, and the company warned that their sales would keep falling.[^1]

findings.title: Most of the lost revenue was purifiers.
findings.text: From fiscal 2004 to 2006 revenue fell by about $235M. By our calculation from the company’s percentages, about $181M of that was the air-purification line.[^1] (derived)

findings.title: It sued its critic, and lost.
findings.text: A federal judge dismissed its suit against Consumer Reports in November 2004, finding no reasonable probability that the reviews were false. The company later paid $525,000 of Consumers Union’s costs.[^4][^5]

findings.title: The founder went, the slide did not stop.
findings.text: Richard Thalheimer left as chairman and chief executive on September 25, 2006. Sales fell another 26% the next year, and the company filed for Chapter 11 in February 2008.[^2][^6][^7]
